analysis.one_liner: Ends Medicare's ban on paying for hearing aids and covers the exams to get them.
analysis.headline: The Medicare Hearing Aid Coverage Act was introduced with 32 bipartisan cosponsors on January 16, 2025, but has sat in two House committees with no hearing, markup, or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law explicitly forbids Medicare from paying for hearing aids or the exams needed to get them, leaving most seniors to pay several thousand dollars out of pocket. This bill deletes that exclusion from the Medicare statute, so hearing aids and related examinations would be covered starting in 2026. It also orders a Government Accountability Office study of existing hearing aid assistance programs. The bill was referred to two House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss — tens of millions of older and disabled Americans. Today the law flatly excludes hearing aids and the exams for them, so beneficiaries pay roughly $2,000–$7,000 per pair out of pocket. If the bill passes, Medicare would cover hearing aids and the examinations to fit them starting January 1, 2026, and the GAO study could push further help for people outside Medicare who also cannot afford aids.

how_it_helps.text: It strikes the legal exclusion at Section 1862(a)(7) of the Social Security Act, which currently forbids Medicare from paying for hearing aids or exams for them.
Coverage would apply to items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2026.
It directs the Government Accountability Office to study hearing aid assistance programs and report to Congress with recommendations for meeting the needs of people with hearing loss.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and federal taxpayers, who would absorb the cost of a new benefit covering hearing aids and exams for tens of millions of beneficiaries. Hearing aid manufacturers and audiologists would gain billed volume, though Medicare payment rates would likely be lower than today's retail prices.

drawbacks.text: Removing the exclusion creates a new mandatory Medicare benefit with no dedicated funding mechanism in the bill, adding to federal health spending and taxpayer costs.

Once Medicare pays for hearing aids, the program's payment rates and rules would govern the market; providers and manufacturers warn that government rates can limit which devices and fittings beneficiaries can access.

The GAO study requirement produces a report 18 months after the effective date — after coverage would already be in effect — so the study informs future changes rather than shaping the initial rollout.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and well-targeted: hearing loss affects a large share of seniors, hearing aids are one of the few major medical needs Medicare flatly refuses to help pay for, and untreated hearing loss is linked to isolation and cognitive decline. The main drawback is federal cost — a new mandatory benefit for tens of millions of beneficiaries is expensive, and the bill does not include a financing mechanism or CBO estimate in the provided record. A second trade-off is that Medicare payment rates could pay providers less than current retail prices, which is good for beneficiaries' wallets but could shrink the number of practices willing to serve Medicare patients. The bill is simple and directly addresses a real gap, but it has received no committee consideration, so its cost and design have not been tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees, but neither committee took it up, so no vote has happened.

narrative.text: The bill's only recorded action after introduction is its referral to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on January 16, 2025.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the action history through the remainder of 2025.
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically still alive but has made no progress since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill, which means Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss keep paying full retail for hearing aids — typically thousands of dollars per pair — and the hearing aid industry keeps selling at retail prices rather than through Medicare rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare beneficiaries keep paying full price

sides.party_line_note: Support is heavily Democratic — 30 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored versus 2 of 223 House Republicans — though a Republican original cosponsor and no recorded opposition make the split softer than a floor vote would show.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would create a new, publicly funded customer base of millions of beneficiaries, though Medicare payment rates would likely be lower than current retail prices. The industry's gain runs alongside beneficiaries' gain.

Coverage of the accompanying examinations plus hearing aids would bring a steady stream of insured patients to hearing care professionals, with Medicare setting payment rates for the first time for these devices and services.

Plans that today advertise hearing aid benefits as an extra perk would lose some of that advantage once original Medicare covers the benefit directly, though many plans would still administer the new coverage.

analysis.trajectory: With a dual referral to two committees and no action after more than a year, the bill's likely path is to die quietly unless its provisions are attached to a larger Medicare or end-of-year health package. An identical proposal passed the House in a prior Congress but never got a Senate vote, so standalone advance again appears unlikely without leadership deciding to prioritize it.
